deep.reconstruction: Context (§§90–93 of E260, Novi Comm. Petrop. 6, 1761). Euler's friction law makes the resistance on a fluid element proportional to the absolute pressure acting on it, including the atmospheric head l of about 30 ft, times the coefficient α. It does not depend on velocity. The resistance per unit length also scales like perimeter/area, which is about 1/g, where gg is the tube's cross-section or g the river depth. For flow down an inclined tube or channel, with ζ the angle to the vertical (so cos ζ = sine of the bed slope), the driving term is cos ζ and the friction term is αl/g. Flow from a vessel of negligible head a can therefore start only if cos ζ > αl/g. Euler sets αl = 0.0075 ft (so α ≈ 0.00025). With z the fall in feet per 1000 ft of channel, the threshold is z_min = 1000·αl/g = 7.5/g. This page tabulates z_min against depth: g from 0.5 to 5 ft in half-foot steps, then 5 to 15 ft in one-foot steps. For example 15.00 ft at 0.5 ft depth, 0.75 at 10 ft, 0.50 at 15 ft. Euler reads it as the critical slope below which a river would stagnate. §93: for slopes above the threshold the velocity head v is given by an exponential law in the channel length b. Its structure is v = a·(decay) + (1 − e^{-αb/g})(g cos ζ/α − l), or as printed with (e^{αb/g} − 1). Two conclusions follow. First, with the slope fixed and cos ζ > αl/g, the velocity grows with the length of the reach. Second, because friction is proportional to absolute pressure, a fall in atmospheric pressure speeds up the river. §94 begins a numerical example: an inclined pipe at 45°, gg = 1/100 sq ft, compared with the horizontal-pipe case of §§86–87.
errors: The table is internally correct: z = 7.5/g to 2 decimals. It truncates rather than rounds in two places: 7.5/4 = 1.875 printed 1.87, and 7.5/12 = 0.625 printed 0.62. 7.5/14 = 0.5357 is printed '0,53½'.

The physical premise is false for water. Friction proportional to absolute pressure, with no dependence on velocity, gives a finite threshold slope below which water stands still. Real rivers flow at far smaller slopes (often well under 1 ft per 1000 ft even at a few feet of depth). The predicted acceleration of rivers when barometric pressure falls is likewise not a real effect.

The velocity formula needs care. Next-page usage (B = 0.7021 = e^{-0.3536}, factor 1 − B = 0.2979) shows the relevant factor is (1 − e^{-αb/g}), approaching a terminal value. The printed form (e^{αb/g} − 1), if read literally, would give unbounded growth with length. Either the print or the transcription has a sign/exponent ambiguity. The term in a should carry the factor e^{-αb/g} rather than appearing bare.

On the next page, the printed bracket (100/√2 − 30) does not reproduce 75.309. The value 0.2979·(g cos ζ/α − l) with g cos ζ/α = 0.0707/0.00025 = 282.8 does give 75.31, so the printed 100/√2 should be 400/√2. Also b = 100√2 should read 141.4, not 14.14.

ideas.what: Critical bed slope for onset of channel flow, inversely proportional to depth, from a velocity-independent wall friction
ideas.modern_name: Yield/threshold criterion sinθ > τ_y/(ρ g h), as for Bingham or Coulomb-type friction flows on an incline
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bingham (1916–22) for yield-stress fluids; its use for mudflows/debris flows is 20th-century (e.g. Johnson 1970, Coussot 1990s)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6, 1761); discussed by Truesdell in his introduction to Opera omnia II.12

ideas.what: Velocity head along an inclined frictional channel relaxing exponentially in length toward a terminal (uniform-flow) value

ideas.what: Dependence of flow rate on atmospheric pressure via pressure-proportional friction

missed.claim: Euler's stagnation table is formally the yield criterion for a viscoplastic (Bingham) layer on an incline. Because atmospheric pressure dominates his pressure-proportional friction, the wall shear is effectively a constant 'yield stress'. That yields exactly the depth-inverse critical slope used today for mudflows and debris-flow deposits. The structure seems not to be remarked on in historical treatments, which treat E260 simply as an unsuccessful theory of water friction.
missed.quote: Pro quauis ergo fluminis profunditate g definire poterimus decliuitatem aluei ... vbi aqua primum fluxum consequatur: ita vt, si decliuitas esset minor, aqua esset stagnatura
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only historiographical: an 18th-century instance of the threshold-slope ∝ 1/depth law of yield-stress geophysical flows. It has no new mathematical content.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a numerical table of a known, physically wrong friction model plus qualitative consequences. The only modestly interesting point is the formal identity with the modern yield-stress incline criterion, which is a retrospective analogy rather than a missed result.
transcription_corrections: In §93, 'si ponatur g=1' is doubtful; it more likely refers to a Fraktur ratio (e.g. 𝔊 = k⁴/g⁴ = 1, outlet as wide as the channel), since g remains a variable in the formula.
The formula is garbled in the transcription; the print appears as v = a ∓ (e^{αb/g} … − 1)(g cos ζ/α − l). Consistency with §95 requires the factor (1 − e^{-αb/g}).
